name: Oral latisse theory

lead: Oral latisse theory is a looksmax.org idea that the lash-lengthening effect of Latisse (bimatoprost) could be obtained by swallowing a similar drug, avoiding the skin-level effects around the eye. The appeal is longer, fuller lashes, which frame the eyes.

The idea is modelled on oral minoxidil, which users say works for more people than the topical form. The thread's reasoning rests on forum explanations of how the drugs work, and no published study has tested an oral bimatoprost approach.

paras: As a theory, it has no established practice. The thread poses it as a question to other members, with replies discussing prostaglandin signalling and blood flow. No protocol is described here.

Bimatoprost is approved as an eye drop or topical lash-base product; its listed effects include eye redness, eyelid darkening and permanent iris darkening. Taking it by another route is untested, and clinicians would be the source for any such question.

angle.text: The theory aims at longer, thicker lashes, which make the eyes look more defined. It proposes a route that would avoid the eyelid-area effects of the topical product; this is a forum idea rather than an established method.

lead: Oral latisse theory is a hypothesis posted on looksmax.org proposing that the eyelash growth of Latisse, the bimatoprost lash product, could be had by taking a related drug orally instead of applying it near the eye [1].

The original poster draws an analogy with minoxidil, arguing that oral minoxidil works for more people than the topical form because it acts systemically, and asks whether the same logic would let someone avoid the periorbital fat loss, eyelid darkening and redness associated with the topical lash product [1].

Bimatoprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog used for glaucoma and approved for cosmetic lash growth; Wikipedia notes that only a small fraction reaches the bloodstream after eye use [2]. No published study has examined an oral version for lashes.
infobox: Lash growth without local side effects

paras: The theory was posted in a looksmax.org thread labelled as a theory. Its author argues that minoxidil works by lowering blood pressure and therefore works best orally, and that Latisse, which the author says lowers pressure in the eye, lengthens lashes as a side effect by extending the hair growth cycle [1]. The author asks whether taking it orally would keep the lash effect while avoiding premature aging of the eye area [1].

A reply in the thread describes Latisse as acting through prostaglandin D2 and notes that prostaglandins regulate blood flow [1]. Other users were tagged for comment. The thread is a discussion of mechanisms rather than a report of anyone's use.

Wikipedia describes bimatoprost as a structural analog of prostaglandin F2-alpha that lowers eye pressure by increasing aqueous outflow, with an approval for hypotrichosis of the eyelashes for cosmetic purposes [2]. Its common effects include eye redness, and it can cause eyelid darkening and permanent iris darkening [2]. Systemic absorption after eye use is small and short-lived [2]. Researchers describe its mechanism as not fully worked out [2].
No studies found on oral bimatoprost or an oral lash-growth approach.
